body:
The meaning and region of Pahari painting

Pahari painting developed in the hill states of the western Himalayas, especially from the 17th to the 19th century. The word Pahari means belonging to the hills.

Important centres included Basohli, Guler, Kangra, Chamba, Kullu, Mankot, Nurpur, Mandi, Bilaspur and Jammu. The tradition developed under the patronage of local rulers and drew upon indigenous painting conventions, with influences from Mughal and Rajasthani art.

Its history is commonly explained through 3 major stylistic phases: Basohli, Guler and Kangra. These are useful for understanding the broad development, although individual artists moved between courts and the boundaries of the styles were not always fixed.

Basohli: Bold colours and expressive forms

Basohli is one of the earliest and most recognisable Pahari styles. It became particularly important in the late 17th century.

Its features include brilliant primary colours, warm yellow backgrounds, forceful outlines, strongly expressive figures and stylised vegetation. Decorative ornaments are also conspicuous.

A significant patron was Raja Kirpal Pal, who ruled from 1678 to 1695. The artist Devida produced an important illustrated series of Rasamanjari around 1694-1695 for this patron.

The Rasamanjari was composed by Bhanudatta. It deals with different types of lovers and emotional situations. Basohli artists used intense colours and expressive compositions to interpret these subjects. The Bhagavata Purana and Ragamala were also illustrated.

Guler: The movement towards delicacy and naturalism

During the early and middle 18th century, painting associated with Guler developed a more delicate and naturalistic appearance. This phase is often called Guler-Kangra or pre-Kangra.

The important artist family of Pandit Seu played a major role in this development. His sons Manaku and Nainsukh became particularly influential.

Manaku is associated with illustrated literary works, including a Gita Govinda series dated 1730. Nainsukh became especially celebrated for sensitive portraits showing the daily life of his patron Balwant Singh of Jasrota.

These portraits record activities such as sitting in a camp, worship and inspecting a building site. Their individuality helps distinguish the Guler-related naturalistic approach from the more stylised Basohli manner.

Raja Govardhan Chand (1744-1773) was an important patron of painting at Guler. The style developed under his patronage and continued through artists associated with the Seu family.

Kangra: Lyrical landscapes and devotional poetry

Kangra painting reached great prominence during the late 18th century, particularly under Raja Sansar Chand (1775-1823).

Artists favoured delicate lines, softly rounded figures, graceful expressions and carefully observed landscapes. Trees, rivers, hills and flowering vegetation became important elements in scenes of devotion and love. Soft greens and blues are especially associated with the lyrical Kangra manner, although Kangra painting was not restricted to these colours.

The school frequently illustrated Gita Govinda, Bhagavata Purana, Ragamala, Baramasa and Bihari Satsai. Radha-Krishna subjects were especially prominent.

Among the important artists associated with the mature Kangra style were Fattu, Khushala and Purkhu. The artistic tradition developed through related families and workshops rather than through a single painter.

How the 3 major Pahari phases differ

PhasePrincipal appearanceImportant association
BasohliBold primary colours and emphatic figuresKirpal Pal; Devida; Rasamanjari
GulerMore delicate modelling and individualised portraitureSeu family; Manaku; Nainsukh
KangraLyrical landscapes and graceful devotional scenesSansar Chand; Fattu; Khushala; Purkhu

The change from Basohli to Guler and Kangra was influenced by contact with Mughal and other painting traditions. However, it is too simple to attribute the entire transformation to the arrival of Mughal painters after Nadir Shah's invasion of Delhi in 1739. Evidence of artistic change in the hill states predates that event, and the development involved several artists and routes of influence.

A connection with Ahmedabad

The N. C. Mehta Collection in Ahmedabad holds examples of Pahari paintings, including a Guler Gita Govinda illustration dated around 1760-1765. This is an important collection connection for Gujarat, but Guler and Kangra are Himalayan painting centres, not Gujarat schools.

Prelims focus

  • Pahari: Western Himalayan hill states.
  • Basohli: Bold colours; Kirpal Pal; Devida's Rasamanjari.
  • Guler: Pandit Seu, Manaku and Nainsukh; more naturalistic treatment.
  • Nainsukh: Associated with portraits of Balwant Singh of Jasrota.
  • Kangra: Sansar Chand; lyrical Radha-Krishna paintings and delicate landscapes.
  • Trap: Rasamanjari is associated with Basohli as well as other schools; the text's name alone does not prove the painting's school.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2026-27, Chapter 5, The Pahari Schools of Painting, pp. 67-79; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, Chapter 9, The Making of Regional Cultures, pp. 129-130, 2020-21 edition.]

body:
The Deccan as a distinct painting region

The Deccani Schools of Painting developed in the courts of the Deccan plateau, especially during the 16th and 17th centuries. Important centres were Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda. Later developments also occurred in Hyderabad and other regional courts.

Deccani painting was supported by the sultans and nobles of the Deccan states. It drew upon Persian artistic influences, local Indian traditions and, to varying degrees, Mughal painting. However, the Deccan developed its own recognisable visual characteristics.

Deccani paintings often combine rich, intense colours with decorative plants, elaborate clothing, courtly figures, imaginative landscapes and a heightened sense of luxury. Golden skies, unusually shaped vegetation and richly patterned architectural settings are characteristic of a number of works.

Ahmadnagar: Early court manuscript painting

Important early examples are associated with the reign of Hussain Nizam Shah I (1553-1565). A manuscript known as Tarif-i-Hussain Shahi celebrates the ruler and contains paintings of royal and historical subjects.

Some Ahmadnagar paintings show a combination of northern Indian figure types and southern clothing conventions. Persian influence can be seen in such features as a high horizon and golden sky. This blending of visual features is important because Deccani painting did not develop in isolation from the rest of India.

Bijapur: Music, literature and brilliant colours

Bijapur was an especially important centre under the Adil Shahi rulers. Two significant patrons were Ali Adil Shah I (1558-1580) and Ibrahim Adil Shah II (1580-1627).

Ibrahim Adil Shah II was closely associated with music and the arts. His literary work Nauras-nama reflects his interest in music.

A major illustrated work associated with Bijapur is the Nujum al-Ulum, dated 1570. This richly illustrated manuscript includes subjects such as astronomical constellations, objects and symbolic representations. Its numerous images demonstrate that Deccani painting was not confined to royal portraits or religious narratives.

Bijapur also produced Ragamala paintings, which transformed musical ideas into pictorial subjects. Its artists employed vivid colours, elongated figures and decorative landscapes.

The painter Farrukh Beg is associated with a well-known image of Ibrahim Adil Shah II playing a tambura, dated approximately 1595-1600.

Golconda: Qutb Shahi court painting

Golconda developed an important painting tradition under the Qutb Shahi rulers. Court scenes, portraits, musicians and richly decorated interiors were important subjects.

A painting titled Dancing before Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, dated around 1590, represents the splendour of the Golconda court. The paintings can feature lavish gold, deep blues, ornamental textiles and carefully arranged architectural spaces.

The Golconda tradition also included poetic and imaginative subjects. Poet in a Garden, associated with the painter Muhammad Ali and dated approximately 1605-1615, is an example.

Why Deccani painting is different from Mughal painting

Both Mughal and Deccani painters represented rulers and court life, and both encountered Persian artistic traditions. Their preferences, however, were not identical.

Mughal imperial painting, especially under Jahangir, is strongly associated with exact portraits and observational studies of nature. Deccani painting often places greater emphasis on intense colour, decorative richness, stylised forms and imaginative courtly settings.

This is a distinction of emphasis. Mughal paintings could also be decorative and symbolic, while Deccani painters could produce convincing portraits and naturalistic figures.

Later continuation

After Mughal expansion into the Deccan during the late 17th century, Deccani painting did not disappear. Related traditions continued under later patrons, including the Asaf Jahi rulers of Hyderabad and other regional courts.

Prelims focus

  • Major centres: Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda.
  • Ahmadnagar: Hussain Nizam Shah I; Tarif-i-Hussain Shahi.
  • Bijapur: Adil Shahi patronage; Nujum al-Ulum, dated 1570.
  • Ibrahim Adil Shah II: Important patron with a strong interest in music; associated with Nauras-nama.
  • Golconda: Qutb Shahi patrons and richly decorated court paintings.
  • Trap: Deccani painting was not merely a branch of the Mughal School; it developed substantial independent regional characteristics.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2025-26, Chapter 4, The Deccani Schools of Painting, pp. 55-66.]

body:
The most useful identifying distinctions

The major miniature painting schools are best distinguished through a combination of region, patronage, subject matter and visual features. A single feature is rarely sufficient because several schools illustrated the same literary works and influenced one another.

SchoolRegion and patronsCharacteristic subjectsStrong identifying clue
PalaBihar and Bengal; Pala rulers and Buddhist monasteriesVajrayana Buddhist manuscriptsFlowing lines; subdued colours; palm-leaf illustrations
Western Indian JainEspecially Gujarat; Jain merchants and donorsKalpasutra and other Jain textsBright red and blue; thin angular outlines; projecting far eye
MughalNorthern India; Mughal emperorsChronicles, portraits, court scenes, animals and plantsRefined portraiture and naturalism, especially under Jahangir
RajasthaniRajasthan courts; Rajput rulersDevotional poetry, epics, portraits and royal activitiesDistinctive local styles, including Kishangarh faces and Kota hunts
PahariWestern Himalayan hill courtsRasamanjari, Gita Govinda, Bhagavata Purana and court lifeBasohli boldness; Guler naturalism; Kangra lyricism
DeccaniAhmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda; Deccan sultansRoyal portraits, Ragamala, music and court subjectsRich colour, elaborate decoration and imaginative landscapes

How to distinguish commonly confused works

Kalpasutra and Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita

Kalpasutra belongs to the Jain tradition and is especially associated with Western Indian manuscript painting. Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita is a Buddhist text and an important example of Pala manuscript illustration.

Ragamala and Rasamanjari

Ragamala paintings represent musical ragas and raginis through pictorial subjects. Rasamanjari, written by Bhanudatta, deals with types of lovers and emotional situations. Both were illustrated in more than one regional painting tradition.

Kishangarh and Kangra

Kishangarh is a Rajasthani school associated with Sawant Singh, Nihal Chand and the celebrated Bani Thani painting. Kangra is a Pahari school associated with Sansar Chand and lyrical Radha-Krishna scenes set in delicate landscapes.

Bundi and Kota

Bundi is especially recognised for romantic landscapes, lush vegetation and literary themes. Kota is particularly celebrated for lively depictions of royal hunting and wild animals. Their artistic traditions are related, so these are useful tendencies rather than absolute boundaries.

Guler and Kangra

Guler is associated with the movement towards delicate modelling and naturalistic portraiture, including the work of Manaku and Nainsukh. Kangra represents a mature lyrical phase, especially under Sansar Chand. These phases are historically connected.

How artistic influences travelled

Indian miniature painting developed through contact as well as regional independence. The earlier Western Indian tradition contributed to the visual language of early Rajasthani painting. The Mughal atelier brought together Persian and Indian artists, and Mughal works subsequently influenced painters in several regional courts.

In the western Himalayan hills, the tradition associated with Basohli developed through the Guler phase into the mature Kangra style. This is a broad artistic progression, not proof that every painting in the region followed one identical pattern.

Gujarat's place in the comparison

Gujarat has a direct historical connection with the Western Indian Jain manuscript tradition, especially through centres of manuscript production, patronage and preservation such as Patan. The N. C. Mehta Collection, Ahmedabad, also preserves examples associated with several other painting traditions.

These are two different kinds of association. Origin and patronage identify where a school developed, whereas a museum or collection identifies where an artwork is preserved. A Kangra painting kept in Ahmedabad remains a Kangra painting.

Do not identify a painting school solely from the religion of its patron or the religious subject depicted. Mughal artists illustrated Indian epics, Deccani painters produced Ragamala paintings, and Rajasthani and Pahari painters illustrated many of the same devotional texts.

Prelims focus

  • Pala: Buddhist manuscript painting; Nalanda and Vikramashila.
  • Jain: Gujarat, merchant patronage and the Kalpasutra.
  • Mughal: Humayun's Persian masters; Akbar's manuscripts; Jahangir's naturalism.
  • Rajasthani: Sahibdin-Mewar, hunting-Kota, Nihal Chand-Kishangarh.
  • Pahari: Kirpal Pal-Basohli, Nainsukh-Guler-related painting, Sansar Chand-Kangra.
  • Deccani: Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda; distinctive sultanate court traditions.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2025-26, Chapter 1, pp. 3-9, and Chapter 4, pp. 55-66; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2026-27, Chapter 2, pp. 10-34, Chapter 3, pp. 35-54, and Chapter 5, pp. 67-79; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, Chapter 9, pp. 128-130, 2020-21 edition.]
